sections.title: How to use this guide
sections.intro: The whole course on one page. Every line with a source chip is a course fact with a verbatim quote; lines without one are study guidance.

items.text: Play the seven steps in order: each one assumes the previous ones. Step 1 needs nothing.
After each step, answer its checkpoint before moving on; the final quiz mixes all seven steps.
Use this page for revision: the reference and small-facts sections hold every definition and number taught in the steps.
Lines marked as our reading (the ride-hailing answers, the conflict rules, R + W > N) are not course statements: do not quote them as the professor's.

sections.title: The route, stage by stage
sections.intro: Five stages from zero to design decisions.

items.text: Stage 1, zero: why databases keep copies. Replication keeps multiple copies of data for availability.
items.quote: Keeping multiple copies of data for availability.

items.text: Stage 2, two ways to organise copies: master-slave (one master accepts writes) and masterless (all nodes accept reads and writes).
items.quote: All nodes accept reads and writes

items.text: Stage 3, what consistency costs: the CAP theorem, the two-phase commit and quorums.
items.quote: A distributed database cannot guarantee all three of these at the same time

items.text: Stage 4, eventual consistency: copies may differ briefly, then converge.
items.quote: Copies may differ briefly, then converge to the same value once replication catches up.

items.text: Stage 5, synthesis: accept a short window of inconsistency for speed, or pay for strict consistency.
items.quote: accept a short window of inconsistency in return for speed, trusting the copies to converge

items.text: Cluster: a set of coordinated servers working together.
items.quote: A set of coordinated servers working together.

items.text: Replication saves multiple copies of data across the cluster, which gives high availability.
items.quote: Replication saves multiple copies of data across the cluster, which gives high availability.

items.text: Master-slave: one master node accepts writes; many slave/replica nodes serve reads.
items.quote: Many slave/replica nodes serve reads

items.text: Masterless: scales writes, not just reads; must handle write conflicts between nodes.
items.quote: Must handle write conflicts between nodes

items.text: Ring: a logical structure for organising partitions, each node linked to its two neighbours; each write goes to the owner and both neighbours.
items.quote: Each write goes to the owning node and its two neighbours, giving high availability.

items.text: CAP: consistency (all servers hold the same, current data), availability (every query gets a response), partition protection (works even if the network splits servers apart).
items.quote: All servers hold the same, current data.

items.text: Two meanings of consistency: transaction consistency (a valid state) and replica consistency (same values on every server).
items.quote: Replica consistency, copies of data on different servers hold the same values.

items.text: Two-phase commit: if either write fails, the whole transaction rolls back.
items.quote: If either write fails, the whole transaction rolls back

items.text: Quorum: the number of servers that must respond for a read or write to count as complete.
items.quote: the number of servers that must respond for a read or write to count as complete

items.text: BASE: Basically Available, Soft State, Eventually Consistent; ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
items.quote: Basically Available · Soft State · Eventually Consistent

items.text: Read-your-writes: once you write a value, your own reads always return it; session consistency limits that to one session.
items.quote: Read-your-writes holds, but only within one session.

items.text: Monotonic read: never an earlier version once seen; monotonic write: writes execute in the order issued.
items.quote: Your writes execute in the order you issued them

sections.title: Small facts: numbers, names, commands
sections.intro: The details that make the difference in a recall question.

items.text: Quorum example on L3#9 uses 5 replicas: read threshold 1 is fastest but may return stale data.
items.quote: With 5 replicas: threshold 1 is fastest but may return stale data

items.text: Read threshold 5 of 5 guarantees a consistent read but is slowest; 3 lets servers agree by majority.
items.quote: A middle value (e.g., 3) lets servers agree by majority

items.text: Write threshold: at least 2, with more replicas than the threshold.
items.quote: Setting it to at least 2 (with more replicas than the threshold)

items.text: L4#39: write to 3 replicas, wait for 2 acks; read waits for 2 matching answers.
items.quote: Write: 3 replicas, wait for 2

items.text: Ring example: keys map to 0-95; 8 servers each own 12 values (S4 owns 36-47).
items.quote: a hash-like function maps each key to 0–95; 8 servers each own a range of 12 values

items.text: Examples: Redis is master-slave, Riak is masterless.
items.quote: Example | Redis | Riak

items.text: Redis lab ports (native): master 127.0.0.1 6379, replicas 6380 and 6381.
items.quote: the master is 127.0.0.1 6379, replicas use 6380 and 6381

items.text: Redis: REPLICAOF NO ONE promotes a replica; INFO replication shows the role.
items.quote: REPLICAOF NO ONE

items.text: Derby sizing: 250,000 score reads per second and 5 writes per second.
items.quote: 250,000 score reads per second and 5 writes per second

items.text: Ride-hailing exercise: the link between the two replicas is cut for 90 seconds.
items.quote: A network fault cuts the link between them for 90 seconds.

items.text: Charlie owes $1,000: discount then order gives $2,000, order then discount gives $1,890.
Causal example: a change to $1,000 lands everywhere before a later change to $2,000.
items.quote: a change to $1,000 lands everywhere before a later change to $2,000

items.text: Masterless conflict scenario time: 21:47:03, journalist A sends 2 to node 1, journalist B sends 1 to node 3.
items.quote: At 21:47:03, journalist A sends match:1001:homeGoals = 2 to node 1

items.text: The CAP theorem's other name: Brewer's theorem.
items.quote: The CAP Theorem (Brewer's Theorem)

sections.title: Traps: where marks are lost
sections.intro: Each trap is a classic confusion from the steps.

items.text: Replicas scale reads, not writes, in master-slave: the single write point is a bottleneck and a risk.
items.quote: Single write point = bottleneck & risk

items.text: Transaction consistency and replica consistency are two different meanings: don't confuse them.
items.quote: Two meanings, don't confuse them

items.text: AP may return stale data; CP blocks some queries instead.
items.quote: Consistent + partition-tolerant, blocks some queries (availability suffers).

items.text: The read threshold trades response against consistency; the write threshold trades response against durability.
items.quote: Write threshold → response vs. durability

items.text: How many replicas (copies) is not the quorum (how many must answer); fewer replicas suit data that is easy to regenerate.
items.quote: Use when data is easy to regenerate and reload.

items.text: Session consistency is read-your-writes within one session only.
items.quote: Session consistency

items.text: In the ring, a failed node's neighbours take over and later send it the writes it missed: no master is elected.
items.quote: S4 comes back: S3 and S5 send it the writes it missed.

sections.title: Night-before checklist
sections.intro: Tick each line only if you can do it without notes.

items.text: I can define cluster, replication, replica and quorum in one sentence each.
I can say when to keep fewer or more replicas, and list the costs of many replicas.
I can compare master-slave and masterless row by row (writes, reads, master fails, node fails, example).
I can walk through the ring example and its node failure in four steps.
I can state CAP, the two meanings of consistency, the two-phase commit and its price.
I can explain both quorum dials with the 5-replica example and the 3-replica, wait-for-2 example.
I can name the five strengths of eventual consistency and redo Charlie's two totals.
I can defend a design for the bank, the cart, the ride-hailing split and the live-score site.

sections.title: Core-first order
sections.intro: Every step is core, so the core-first order is the A-to-Z order itself. If you have only one evening, do steps 4 to 6 after a five-minute look at step 1: they carry most of the definitions.

items.text: 1. Replication and how many replicas (step 1).
2. Master-slave replication (step 2).
3. Masterless replication and the ring (step 3).
4. CAP, two meanings of consistency and the two-phase commit (step 4).
5. Quorums: read and write thresholds (step 5).
6. ACID versus BASE and the strengths of eventual consistency (step 6).
7. Synthesis scenarios (step 7).
